blocks.x: You want to rest a minute? You asked a question and I start talking.

Yeah, that's alright. You have to give your name first so you'll know who's talking. In here? Yeah, I think it'll pick it up. Leave it right down. I think it's getting up there. It'll pick it up right there. Okay.
My name is Uriel Wilford Montgomery.
When were you born? You can just sit back and relax. It'll pick up anything in the moment. I was born in 1906, April 18th. Now, where were you born?
Kentwood, Louisiana.
Kentwood.
That's 83 miles north of New Orleans on the Illinois Central.
Right up on the, above Hammond, up that way. That's right. Can you remember the first music you ever heard? Were your parents, for instance, musicians?
Well, I had a uncle, great uncle, my father's uncle. He had a band. His name was Gunsey Montgomery. He had the big four band out of Norleene, Louisiana.
Yeah. And what did he play?
Well, he played practically every instrument in the band.
That was a regular dance band then, was it?
Was it a Surnate band, dance band, like so forth. Yeah.
And you heard them then when you were?
Oh, around four or five years old, something like that.
Any of your other folks play or sing? Well, my father, he played carnet.
My mother, she played accordion. All my sisters were piano players and brothers also.
About how many brothers and sisters did you have?
It was ten in all, five girls and five boys. Yeah.
And they all played something then? It was really...
All played. My older brother, he played, uh, carnet, too. Mm-hmm. I used to play a bass tuba.
And what was your very first instrument that you started on? Piano.
On piano.
Did you take any lessons or just pick it up yourself or some of your sisters or brothers?
No, I picked it up myself. I was practically the first one in the family to learn how to play.
Were you older than the, uh, most of the others or one of the younger?
No, I have, I have two brothers older than me and, uh, three sisters. Yeah. All of them.
Um, what was the first music you heard, do you think, in your home? Do you remember? Was it someone singing or? Well, no. Well, practically all of my people, they could sing.
They were, belonged to church, and they were choir people.
Which church did you belong to?
Temple, Chapel Baptist Church.
Baptist Church, yeah. And, uh, that was up there in your hometown? That was in my hometown. How long did you, uh, live there before you left home?
Well, I ran away from home when I was 11 years old. 11?
Where did you go?
Well, I went to Hammond, Louisiana. I went to Hammond, Pontchartula, Tall Benny, Holton, Holton, Louisiana. I went out there, I got a job out there playing.
You could play pretty good piano then, I guess, at 11, huh? Oh yeah.
Well, I played good enough to hold a job. Ten dollars a week, room and board.

Yeah. How old did you start? When were you? Well, I started playing when I was around five. About five. By 11 you'd been playing six years. Yeah. What type of music did you play then? Mostly blues or other music?
No, I played any type of music, you know. Uh, commercial, such as numbers like Minky, Pretty Minky, and different numbers like that. Yeah. Blues, too.
Did you sing, too, with your piano, or mostly just blues?
Well, I started singing when I was about 12. I always could sing, though, but I mean, I...
Yeah, sure.
But, you know...
Who were some of the first singers you heard? Can you remember any famous blues singers or anyone coming here?
Well, the first two blues singers that...I mean, two record...recording singers that I remember of ever hearing were Edith Wilson and Mamie Smith.
Yeah. What kind of voice did Mamie have in those days? On her old records, it's hard to tell.
She had a kind of light voice. A keen voice.
Did you ever hear Ma Rainey in those days?
Oh, yeah, I heard Ma Rainey. In fact, it was I worked with her later on here. Well, you worked with her? A couple of days.
Did you travel with her show? Did she have a show?
No, I played a...one...a couple of shows with her. I played one at the Grand Theatre on 31st and State.
Yeah.
That was up in the later years.
When did you first get to New Orleans?
Oh, I was in New Orleans when I was seven or eight years old.
When you got down in the morning. Can you remember what kind of music you heard there? Any of the bands or piano players? Oh, yeah.
I heard Buddy P.T. play. I heard the Silver Leaf Band they had in New Orleans at the time.
What was the Silver Leaf?
Dance? They were a dance band. Dance band. And also I heard Chris Kelly.
Yeah.
Kid Nichols. Who was Kid Nichols?
He's a trumpet player too. He's a trumpet player too. Um... Did you work in New Orleans then pretty early too?
Well, I worked in New Orleans when I was around 17 and 18 years old.
Did you play with bands or piano?
Well, I played some with Sam Morgan's band. And also I played some with Kid Clayton. He's a trumpet player.
Oh, yeah.
He's still there.
Yeah. Yeah, he's still playing. Doing quite well. Um... You once made a tour, didn't you, with Desdune?
Yeah, well I played with Clance Desdune's band. He was out in New Orleans. Yeah.
Did you play with him in the city too? Oh, yeah.
We played at Pelican, Estor, and then out. Out of town. Yeah.
Who else was in that band that you remember? He played trombone, didn't he?
Oh, he played violin.
Violin? Oh, I thought he was a trombone player. No, no.
He played violin. I see. Let me see who all were in the band. Me and Raymond Johnson.
What did he play?
Raymond Johnson played trombone.
Trombone.
Raymond Brown, that was it. Oh, Raymond Brown. Raymond Brown, he played trombone. And Harry Faganatou played banjo.
What's that name again?
Harry Faganatou. He had a French name.
Yeah, there was French names, didn't there? Yeah.
And Oliver Alcon. Oh, yeah. Alvin Alcon. Well, George McCullin were first, and then Alvin taking his place.
Oh, yeah.

Alvin Alcon, George, and Shine, the drummer they call Shine. Oh, yes. He was playing drums with us. And Pop Kimball, he was a bass, tuba player. Yes. Let's see. Hal Desjohn, he was a saxophone player. Oh, yes. He's still there. And Lucian Johnson was a saxophone player. They had a reed session.
Big band then, wasn't it?
Yeah. Fourteen pieces.

About what date was that? I mean, or what years? How old were you when you were with Desden? Well, that was around 1928. When did you leave on tour with him? Right away then, after that? Well, I left after then with him.

We toured all through Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Illinois, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Michigan. And we made, we played Oklahoma also. Played a few dates over in Dakota, South Dakota, across from Sioux City, Iowa.
And you remember the earliest piano players that you heard in New Orleans? Did you hear any of the players in the district, for instance?
Well, practically I knew practically all the old timers around. Steve Lewis. Yeah. Walter Pigeon, Fats Pigeon, and Red Caillou, Udell Wilson.
Yeah.
And Poiré Nolan, Little Willie, Little Dookie, Little Sammy.
Little Sammy. Were some of those fellows mostly blues players, or did they play ragtime? Well, they played ragtime. Jazz, jazz piano.
All sorts. All sorts. Did you hear Manuel Moneta?
Do you remember him?
I didn't ever remember him in person.
He's been teaching mostly across the river, so hasn't played much in late years. Did all of the bands use piano mostly, or some of the bands? Not at that time.
I know, didn't. Just a few bands used piano. Well, Pierone, Steve Lewis was playing with him. Yeah. Fate Marble, he was a piano player. Yeah. He had a band, he had the band on the boat.
Yeah.
Stimma Capital.
What kind of a pianist was Fate? He was a good pianist. He was nice at the time.
And Udell, at the time, he was about one of the best around in New Orleans, Udell, I think his home was in Kansas City.
Yeah, I think, I think I heard that too. What does Steve Lewis' style like? I know it's hard to explain just by words, but still.
He was a good piano player too. He played kind of on the order of Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll Mug.
Did you hear Jelly Roll any place in your travels?
Oh yeah, I heard him in Chicago. In Chicago, yeah.
I knew him, got to hear him. He was wonderful I thought too. Anything else about those early pianists that you can remember?

Well there were some great piano players down through and some of the greatest, one of the greatest piano players ever I looked at was Cooney Vons. He was from Hattiesburg, Mississippi. And they had another one there they called Blind Jug. He was a good. And also another one they called Gus Permer. He was great. Yeah.
Well, what about some of the bands, what type of music did they play when you heard them?
Oh they played jazz. Jazz. I thought he put tea, have you any recollection? He was jazz trumpet player, he was one of the greatest. He and Rainey, Kid Rainey.
Yeah you heard of Rainey.
Well Lee Collins, he was good too. Lewis, he was good. Well at the time Lewis had left too, him and Joe Oliver who came up.
Yeah. Yeah. Did you hear any of the street bands, the parades? Oh yeah.
Well on carnival day or something like that, that's when you hear the majority of the bands at the time, so because they were all be on the corner in a truck or something, you know, Balli Hood. Yeah.
Did you ever play any other instrument in the parade, that is you said you played tuba once?
Well I played tuba in some few parades, you know, not in New Orleans and other cities like Jackson. Different places.

Now you seem to have gotten around the country a lot more than a lot of the fellas, at least that are still there. I wondered, you've probably heard a lot of other small bands all over the south there. Oh yeah. How did they compare with New Orleans? Did they have about the same style or did they seem to...

Oh they played good. We had a little gang of kids there in Bogalusa, Louisiana to play nice. The Rhythm Aces they called them. The fact of the business I started one or two boys out with the, you know, the founder of the band. Yeah. Willie Esther and among them.
Do you remember anybody else in that band? What?
The Bogalusa band? Oh yeah. They had Hanson Sevier. He was a good piano player. He used to be piano player in the band. Well some of the boys I just remember their names.
Yeah. Some of those fellas might still be up there though.
They might still be there.
Can you tell us about some of the records? Those old Bluebird records or the very first records you made?
The very first records I made was with singer Irene Scruggs. They called it Chocolate Brown. She was out of St. Louis. She has a daughter over in Europe called Baby Scruggs. She's a showgirl now.
That's her name. What label was that for?
That was on Paramount.
Was Mayo Williams with Paramount then or who had you?
He wasn't with Paramount. Art Labley was with Paramount.
Where did you make those? Up here?
Out at Grafton, Wisconsin. Wow.
That was your first date then? That was the first date. Can you remember the first records you made then when you'd sing or play or?
Well she was singing. I was there in the playing.
I mean when you made under your own name you might say. Well that was for Paramount too.
I made No Special Rider Blues and Vicksburg Blues on Paramount label.
And that was up in Grafton too? That was in Grafton. Do you remember the year about?
That was 1929.

29. And the Bluebird records were those your next ones? The seventh된 stuff withStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStługStług
or was there anything else? Well, no, the next company I worked for was Vocalion and Brunswick.
Yeah.

I made Louisiana blues for Vocalion and Brunswick. They had, I think they had three labels, melaton, Vocalion, and Brunswick. Yeah. But I made a lot of numbers with Irene Scruggs, St. Louis Woman Blues, Bar It Love, and Got to Get Mine in Front, Good Meat Grindr, and so forth like that. I just remember.
Did you use guitar on some of those records? Just me on the cymbals. I'm singing as well. Vicksburg Blues, can you remember when you wrote that or why you wrote it?
Around 19, well, I was fooling around with it since 1923.
Mm-hmm.

Well, we started playing it around, you know, Fairty, Louisiana, Natchez, Mississippi, Tallulah, Louisiana, different places, you know, just Kepa color-vading it, you know. So I named it. Some of the boys tried to make 44 blues out of it, so I just changed the name of it because we made it up. Me and two more boys, Friday and Dale Coe Robert. So I changed the name to Vicksburg Blues, you know, I have to.
Yes, sir.
I think you tried.
Did you ever live in Vicksburg? Oh, yeah.

Long? I played in Vicksburg. At the Princess Theater. I played 1014 Washington Street at Zach Luris' Nightclub. Played down to Steamboat Exchange, down to Fitzgerald, they called it. A lot of places. Yeah. Bells Cafe. How long did you stay?
When you go to a town like that, did you stay?
Well, I stayed in Vicksburg for a couple of years. I used to play at Henderson, Royer Garden, and Fairty, Louisiana.
What kind of bands were up there? Did they sound about the same kind of jazz they played in New Orleans, or?
Well, no, they mostly had string bands all up through there. Bud Scott had the best band around up through there, from Natchez, Mississippi. Then they had a lot of...
Was that the Bud Scott that was with Kidore and went to Chicago?
No, that wasn't the same one. He had a string band, this Bud Scott. Bud Scott also played guitar.
That's what I got wondering.

Well, this one he played a mandolin. And he was a wonderful singer. He had a lot of good musicians, but they were string instruments. Mark Hawkins, Forrest Hawkins, Bubba Quirk, Walter, and the gang, you know, they all played the bandolons, guitars, and the first one thing I liked.
It wouldn't have been Little Walters up here at the Harmonic. Not this one, no. You played, you said, in Natchez too, a while? Oh, yeah.
Well, I played in Natchez quite a bit. Different times.

Were there many, just the blues singers that would go around in those days that drop in the places, or did they really hire the singers? I mean, I know you were hired a professional musician, but I mean-
Well, mostly that people that got jobs like that in those bell houses, they call them, hockey tanks, were piano players. Well, they didn't hire anybody else, you know.
I wondered if a lot of guitar-
Later on up in the year, they'd hire a drummer with you, you know.
I just wondered if there'd be a lot of singers just dropping in and singing a number or two, or-
Well, you have plenty of that all the time.

What are those barrel houses like? I mean, were they about the same as the Honky Tonks and all in New Orleans, or- Well- What hours did you play? I mean, if you remember a little bit about the life in those places- Yeah, I was- The hour that you worked-

Yeah, I was in a lot of those places. You start to work around nine o'clock, and you play till the day the next morning, you know, on the Sunday morning, that's on weekends on Saturday night. Well, through the week you start playing around seven, eight o'clock, and you're off around ten, ten thirty. Because most of the places on them jogged there to close up so the people could go to wake, you know. Yeah.
You hear stories about the lumber camps and all, like a lot of the blues things are called-
I played on a lot of lumber camps, logging camps too.
You know, what would happen there? I mean, you weren't working there in the camp or anything, you'd just go there and play?

No, I was living there playing. I used to play on Barth camp for a guy they called Gold Mine. That was a logging camp. Well, I got twenty-five dollars a week room and board. I stayed on the place. Yeah. I played for Curtis Coleman and Barth in the same camp.
Where was that, up in Mississippi or Louisiana?
That was up in Mississippi. Down in Bush, Louisiana, that's down below Boagalusi, played out there on that camp for Tom Payne. A guy, he run the place by the name of Tom Payne.
At those camps, I mean, when would you play? Would they have sort of a bar room there?
Well, they'd have music practical every night. They would dance along.
Were there women around, a lot of women around the camp too, or how did that? Oh, yeah. See, I don't know anything about those long camps.
Yeah, there'd be plenty of women. There'd be some fine ones around there too. Yeah. Kind of love them. And most of them loved the dance, you know.

Yeah. A real camp, excuse me for keep talking about it since I don't know about it, I want to find out. Did they move those camps around when they, say, cut down a lot of the forest? Did they move it over? What did they have? Tents or cabins?

They had little houses, shacks like they called them. They put them up on flat cars, you know. Take a crane and pick them up. Oh, yeah. Set them up on the flat car and move them to the next place. So they'd move those around the country then? Move them around the country.
As they'd go into a new timbers actually. That's right. And then you'd stay with the camp there and just play music on every night?

Well, not exactly. Sometime I'd go to another camp or another town or go to like Bogalusi or play there. I used to play in Bogalusi too. And also I'd play around Jackson, Mississippi, Meridian, Hattiesburg, Natchez, Vicksburg, different places like that. Cholula, Louisiana, Faraday, Louisiana.
Remember much about Hattiesburg. Are there bands up there? Would there be any musicians left there from New Orleans maybe that moved up that way and stayed, do you think?

Well, I don't think so. Lee used to be around there. He and Edmund Hall also. Oh, yeah. They were there with Cooney Vons. Lee Collin, he stayed around there. And also Edmund Hall. They had a band there. They'd go about, you know, like Birmingham, Mobile. Yeah. And still living.
Yeah. Did you ever work along the Gulf Coast very much? Biloxi and Mobile?
Oh, yeah. I played Biloxi, past Chris Dad, Gulfport. I used to live in Gulfport on 30th Avenue.
Yeah. When you lived there, what would you, did you play just solo piano or sing?

Yeah, I was, I had a drummer, that's all. And I... Not a band though? I played, across the brights they call it, at Curtis Coleman's place. They had three or four different places there. Johnny Hopper had one, Milton had one, different people had places. Mm-hmm.
Did you ever hear many minstrel shows or other traveling tent shows that would come around? Or did you ever work with any of those? There were a lot of...

Well, I never did care too much for working on the shows, but I had a lot of friends that did work on them. I remember Georgia Smart Set, Silas Green, and also the Georgia Minister, Rabbit Foot. That was the one Jalee Davis was on, Sweet Papa Snowball they call it, he was on Rabbit Foot. That's through the running, I think. Yeah, they had Carter and Poe Gibson. And then, uh, Holkamp, he had, uh, Georgia Smart Set. Yeah. I had a lot of boys. I, uh, I, uh, organized a band with some of the boys out of that, when the show went, you know, bomb, I ordered, I made up a band with, uh, some of the boys out of the show. Doc Pomley, Luke Pomley, those two brothers, they were on the, Georgia Smart Set.
Did those shows, uh, just travel mostly in the summertime and what they do in the winters?
Well, they, they put up in the runters, you know, head caught in some place.
How long would they stay in that place? One night stands or a week or usually or what?
Well, most, uh, it was one night stands, one nighters.
Mm-hmm. Um, did you ever hear Bessie Smith when she was traveling around or up here in Chicago?

Oh, yeah. I heard her, I heard her around. Well, I heard, frankly, all of the people that traveled. I heard Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith. I saw them and, uh, Ida Cox and Ma Rainey and Butterbean and Susie. Mm-hmm. Well, I said, well, at the Lyric Theater, you used Ethel Waters, you'd see all of those. Yeah. Practical, along back. It was located on Apperville and Paganda in Orleans.
Yeah, it's not there now, but I've heard of you. Yeah. Um, who were your very favorite blues singers? If you had to pick somebody that you enjoyed more than anybody?
Bessie Smith.
Bessie Smith. Did you ever hear of many men blues singers? There were some of the ones like Blind Lemon. Did you ever hear him from Texas? Did he get around?

Yeah, but I never did care nothing about his singing or whatever. I mean, maybe he was a good singer, but I never did care for it, because he always didn't sing on time. He'd break his time, pretty much, you know. Yeah. Alonnie Johnson was my singer back in that, for blues, back at that, in those days. In fact, it had been to see what tops at the time.
Yeah. Um, who would you say is your favorite piano player, if you had to pick somebody, one or two of them?

Well, nobody, a lot of people never heard of the one I was speaking of, Cooney Vons. He was the best one I've ever heard, from Hattiesburg. What's the first name again? Cooney. Cooney. Cooney Vons. That was his name.

Yeah. Um, can you tell me something about the style of blues up here in Chicago? They began calling it Boogie Woogie piano, like Pinetop and all those numbers. And the Pinetop's Boogie Woogie. Did they ever play that style based down south?

Well, that's practically all we played. You'd have to play that style for people to dance by. On blues, except you played a mighty good beat, slow blues, because most of the time, Jooks, Balleisers, people danced, you know. Yeah. Well, that's mostly we played, but we didn't call it Pinetop's Boogie Woogie. We didn't call it Boogie Woogie at all. They called it Dudlow Joe.
Dudlow Joe. Dudlow Joe. That was the style of the bass, you mean, isn't it? That's right. Rolling bass and different types. Oh, Cal Cal Davenport, when did you first hear him or meet him?
Well, I met him around in 1928 and 9, around Chicago, yeah. What's it called? At the Old Angelus building now, 35th and Wabash. That's where we were located at the time. Of course, it's called now.
You did hear that Boogie bass and style then down south?
Oh, we were playing that way before it came out already. We were playing all those kind of basses down there.
Yeah. Can you remember the very first time you heard that style, or was it so far back you can't even remember?

Well, most youngsters would play that style that were learning how to play. Even when you started playing? Because it wasn't complicated for you to stretch your hand. You could just play with two or three notes. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da like that, you know. See, I mean, you didn't have to stretch your hand if it wasn't large enough, you know. So, fact of the business, I've been playing it ever since I was around eight, nine years old.
Did you enjoy playing in bands more or working as a single?

Well, I used to enjoy working by myself more than I did with bands and things. But now I'm getting kind of used to fooling with bands. I play with them a little more longer, you know, than I ever did, so it's getting coming kind of natural to me to play with bands. I would get with bands, stay with, be with bands six or eight months, and then I'd leave them, you know, maybe three or four months. I've been with a lot of bands, different ones. But I never did care to make it my career, you know. I've owned the band. I've had pretty good outfits myself.
Yes, I know you have. Can you tell me a little bit about ragtime style, where you first heard the, you might call the ragtime style, like maple leaf and those kind of rags?

Well, fact of the business, I've never heard maple leaf too good to re-reglect it now. I don't know so much about it, but the first rag that I ever remember learning were, were 12th Street rag. I was a youngster then, around eight, nine years old.
The solo you played quite often, the mule face blues. Where did you learn that?

Well, I learned that often in orchestration. That was a band number. Yeah. And we had it in several bands that I worked in. So, it was complicated for the majority of musicians to play it. Trumpet players. Yeah.

trombone players and everything, practically every band that get it was hard for them to play because it was kind of funny, you know, and every band that got a hold to it didn't care about fooling with it, you know. So I just took it up on myself to learn the whole thing by myself, you know. So some bands could play pretty good.
Yeah, Oliver made a record of it.

Well it's King Oliver's numbers, he wrote it, yeah. So well he had it kind of complicated for musicians at the time, of course today it wouldn't be too much from the play, it wouldn't be nothing because they're more experienced, you know, in the reading abilities anyway. So that's what made it hard. It took a pretty good reader, sight reader to read it, played good. So I'd taken it up on myself, I learned it off of the orchestration, you know.
Are there any pianists that you might say influenced your style after you got more experience that you listened to and you say you picked it up mostly yourself and your brothers and sisters?

Well I mostly play like myself because I used to listen to Earl Hines, I think he's one of the greatest jazz piano players with a band that you could afford today, even until today. I used to listen to him, I used to have ideals from him, I listened to him a great deal. But I mostly play by myself, I can't, I mean like myself, I can't hardly play like nobody. Since I've been playing so long.
Do you enjoy playing blues a lot? Some players, I think other blues are so old that they just get tired and sick of playing them, but you still enjoy playing blues, don't you?
No, I wouldn't. Really? No, I don't care so much for playing them. At times I like to play them and again I don't like even him, less mostly. So, I don't care so much for them.
You'd rather play other pieces then?
Other, no.
Is there anything else about your life? I don't want to keep you along, I know you're not long. Is there anything else that you'd like to...
Well, not exactly.
To say or add to what we've talked about?
Well, I believe that would be about all of them.
You were going to say something else there?

Yeah, well I was going to speak about some musicians. Still around that way, down around New Orleans, Jackson, Mississippi there. They got Doc Pomler, he's a mighty good trumpet player. He's in Jackson still. Jackson. His brother, he's a good bass, tuba player. Edmund Pomler, his name, we call him Luke. His name's Edmund Pomler. Also, they got one of the world's greatest show drummers around there, Joe White.
So well, yes, I've heard of him. Well, he's in Jackson. He's in Jackson.
Think he's still there?
I think he's still there. He played New Orleans too, didn't he?
Oh yeah, he played all around.
I guess most of those fellows. We'll have to get up to Jackson sometime. Yeah, that's right. Interview those people.
So, Luke, Edmund Pomler has a cafe there on Oakland and Mill Street.
What is that last name?
Edmund Pomler. Pom? P-E-R-M-I-L-E-Y.
I thought at first it said Palmer maybe. Pomler. Pomler. Well, maybe we can get up there and see those fellows and talk to them too and interview them later. That's right.
So they're good.
Do you remember anybody else in Hattiesburg that might be there? Or Bogalusa?
Well, I think they all did. Or Bogalusa. They died out there. Emile Thomas, he were there, but he passed here not so awfully long ago.
Anybody in Bogalusa or?

Well, most of those who have left, they had Sabadeo Arty. He was a pretty good piano player, but I think he lived at, past Christian now. He moved over from Bogalusa. Martin Davis, he was a, Martin Davis, he was a pretty good piano player. He lived in Hattiesburg. So I think they mostly, some in California.
Anybody up Baton Rouge, Wade, did you ever work up there much, Alexandria?

Well, I knew a few people around Baton Rouge. They used to have one of the good bands out of Baton Rouge. They called Toot Johnson. Yeah. Well, I remember Guy Kelly, he was from Baton Rouge, and also Johnny Handley. He's a clarinet player. He used to be around Baton Rouge. He used to be with Toot Johnson, but I think his home was up around past Christiane and Gruffville. He should be, still be around in Orleans. Johnny Handley. Clarinet player.
Oh yes, that's right, sure. Yeah. Yeah, he is there. He plays street bands all the time. Yeah. In the parades.
And I know Joe Robichaud, he and I are good friends.
Yeah, he was up here, he'll be here in two weeks and uh...
Yeah. Also, George Lewis, he and I are good friends.
George Gano. George Gano, that's my buddy.
Yeah, he used to wake me up there. Where did he work with you?
He worked all over with me.
We, you know, we had a traveling band. We had quite a jackson. He played all around with me.
Yeah. Well, I won't keep you any...
And I know Brother Al Wynn, he's a good trombonist, Lee Collier.
Yeah, all those fellows you've worked with up here in the city now in Chicago.
Yeah. We got a lot of good musicians around here too, you know. Paul King, Overtree. Got a lot of...
Yeah, quite a few. Raymond Waters.

And I got a... still got a friend, he's my blues singer still, my guitar player, Big Bill Brunzi. I got to go see him. I'm going by too, maybe Sunday. Yeah, I promised to go see him the other day, I didn't get...
He's able to have a visitor, I guess. Oh, yeah.
Can't talk much though, I guess.
Oh, he can't talk so much.
But he'll talk, he'll talk, I keep him laughing all the time.
I'll go by and say hello to him. He's not too sick to him, one company then, anyway. That's right. That's right. Well, that's... Yeah, that's right. That's something else to add.
Of course, our boy is sick too, I feel sorry for him, you know, but I can't do... Lee Collins.
Yeah, Lee, I'm going to try and see him. Well, I think then we'll let you run along as soon as I get a picture of you. Oh, sure. There were a couple more names you wanted to add there, right?

Yeah, and they had a piano play along, yes, when I was a little boy riding all these, was a great... When they... his name was Ford, I didn't never know his other name. Ford. That was his name, and then they had another one played in Boca Lucey, they called Charlie Mahana, he was a great, great blues player. And No Leg Kenny, he didn't have any legs. His legs was up off to his knees, you know.
Oh, he got around all right though.

He got around, he was a good piano player. He used to play around Oakdale, the Louisiana, and the Quince. He was up there. We have a great piano player who lived in Beaumont, if he's not dead, they called Lee Johnson, David Lee Johnson. And Peg Top, the guy, the guy they called Peg Top, he was a great piano player. And around Chicago, we used to have a lot of good blues pickers around here too, you know. Forty-Five, the guy, his name was Forty-Five, and Albert Ammon.
Yeah, yeah, I knew Albert.
Well, Jimmy Hanson, he still was in the crew. He played the blues, and we had Chicago Bill here, he was good, also. Kyle-Kyle Devon, boy, he was living around, and Cripple Clance Lawson.
Yeah, Clarence died, and he was gone.
He was way back, and we had Jerome Carlton around, he was great at the time. Oh, Father Hyde, he had to be great, he was there.
Yeah.
Teddy Wilson was around here a while back, you know. All those were great.
I got a quick picture of him over there.
And we still got a Henry Pomeroy, the guy wrote the number, I found a new baby.
Oh, yeah.
And Henry Shane also, the one who wrote Mr. Freddie's blues, he's still around, I see him around.

You can talk, I asked about either Louis Armstrong or Jimmy Noon, some of the other bands. Yeah.

Well, I just returned from St. Louis working a season on the boat with Charlie Crep. And things were pretty bad musically in Chicago at that time. And Louis was here, and he was just beginning to reach his popularity. He was just beginning to get into it. So he got an idea to get a band, form a band, and lease several dance halls, and this alternate weekly. Yes.
Like that.

So he leased the hall on 47, the old Warwick Hall. Oh yeah, I remember. And he got another hall on the west side. I don't remember, it was on Madison Street somewhere, I don't remember just the name of it. So he got a band together. I was in the band, Zooty, and Earl, Joe Walker, Lil' Joe Walker, Frank Sacks, and another boy, George Terence, was on Sacks. Was Lil in the band? No, Lil wasn't in the band, no. He was still married to Lil, but Lil wasn't in his band. Earl was there. Oh, that's right. That's right, true. I don't remember if we had a guitar or not. It possibly could have been packed by, I doubt it, I think we had a tuba. We had seven pieces, I know. I think it possibly could have been Peter Briggs. So that was his idea. I mean we were going to make our own work, you know, and be independent and one of those things. But it didn't turn out quite that way. I mean we worked, we would have a few people out. Because Lil wasn't really too popular, he was on his way up, you know, just another name. So we would play these halls, if he had at least. And the way he had it figured out, we had about four nights. We had about three nights that he was actually promoting, and several other nights that we could fill in the week in order to make a week. But on his deals, the crowd didn't come out. I mean we tried it all for a period of about a month.
I remember Zutty told me years ago, he said in place of being the hot six, they thought they'd better call it the hungry six.
Yeah, that's just our poor. And they were so nice at the end of the night, there wouldn't be any money to split.
I think you said Lil had the Hawker jewelry to keep things going or something.

Yeah, maybe. Some story. In fact, I think Lil did finally come into the band after I cut out and then Earl cut out and they still tried to carry on. So what happened, the people didn't come out, didn't support it. I remember what really topped off everything. He gave a dance free at Warwick Hall, you know. He said, well I just want to see if we can do it. Let's come on in, it's for free, no animation done. Let's come on in. He didn't expect to make anything. So we couldn't have a crowd for free, you know. They didn't come in for free. They didn't come in for free. You know, free. Everything for free. Let's come on in. So they didn't come in. So that's when he threw up both hands and said, well, it don't look like this is it. And of course he was stuck with the lease and everything. He eventually had to pay it off. So that venture didn't work out at all. So Dave Payton had a job. He was for a band going out here at 63rd in the Persian Hotel. He was a club Baghdad at that time. He was following, oh what's this for? He did so much, he had a terrific swing band. He did so much for jazz and everything. Most of the musicians come up on them. And stuff like
He was a drummer. From the old school Bixen, Benny Goodman, and all of them.
Ben Pollitt.

Ben Pollitt. So he had this job to going out there following Ben Pollitt. So he had contacted me, Earl, Louie, and Zutty. We were supposed to go in there together with the rest of the band to make up the band. So last minute different things come up. Louie had offered to go with Clarence Jones at the Metropolitan Theater. So Louie went there, and Earl went someplace else. So Zutty and I, we're going out here with Dave Payton. But that was the end of that deal with Louie's band. And of course, I think it was before then, I got a band. Yeah, it was before then. I got a job at a place at 22nd Street between State and Wabash. It was Midnight Frolics at that time.
Was that still the district up there?

That was the district. That was the last. That was the last. The district was fading, but there still was a slight resemblance of it. I mean Bloom, the name of Artie Bloom I think still had the Frolics there. And well of course they had terrific shows and they had big shows. Ralph Edwards had the house band there. So they wanted a band just to play at animation time. So what happened, this, before then they had a lot of flow entertainers, you know, with the small pianos and the girl singers. They would push them all around and doing the animation they would sing. So he got the idea that he wanted some real jazz music in there instead of entertainers. So I had my to get connection for the thing. This same fellow who was a very good friend of mine from the All of Us drummer, Francois Mosley, his brother was a caretaker and pulled her there for the place. So when the man come up with the idea, he shoots it right on to me. So I go down and talk with the fellow. Well he was set on Earl. Who he really wanted was Earl Heinze. So he said, well I will give you this job if you can get the Earl Heinze. So I said, well I doubted very much. I said, I think it's almost impossible. I think it's just about impossible to get Earl. But I said, there's another real great jazz artist that I can get. Song sure I could get him. Why I knew I could get Lurie, because Lurie was working at the Vendome Theater, see. He was in the pit with Erskine Tate at that time. And they were through about a quarter to eleven or something like that. Well now and then we didn't start until eleven or eleven fifteen or something like that. So that would be a double for him, see. So I talked this fellow into him, I said well just hear the outfit if you don't like it. There's nothing lost but a little time. So he said okay. So I got Lurie and this boy that had been in Lurie's band, George Terence and little Joe Walker. I got Peck on guitar and this boy, the drummer. The drummer from the All-Irland Service. I was just talking about his brother worked in the play. Mosley. Mosley, Francois Mosley and myself. And we went down there, Lurie was really blowing there. So we went down there and made the audacious man and said yeah this is it, this is great, this is great. So we start to work there. We start to work there and everybody's real happy. It's a terrific spot. I mean the place is packed in the jam all the time. It's a lively crowd and everything. So we do about two weeks there. And one night in the middle of the night everybody struck in the place. Say if you keep, if you keep that band there we all would walk out. All the electric, the electricians and the waiters and everything. I mean it was just one of those things. Because during that time there was a friction between, they say you trying to bring 35th street to 22nd street. There was a friction between number 10 and 208. And of course he had laid off, that was in the Spoden district, and he had laid off a lot of these girls, singers who was Dublin and a lot of the regular fellas around there had laid off. So they were all hot about those things. So in the middle of the night, I mean everybody said well this is it. The whole thing stopped. The place is packed in jam. And all people used to come out of here. And then Sophie Tuck and all of them, they were in town. They would be there every night. And the food was blowing. There wasn't any question. It was a man saying well what can I do. You see what's happening. You see what's happening. So he was nice enough. He said I'll give you boys two weeks out. He paid us for two weeks. He was the most hype person because he liked, I mean when we went in there it was in the winter time and he'd show us where our showers and everything was for the summer. You know. And everybody said well look like we set. You know. And this incident had to happen. So he was nice enough which he didn't have to do. He paid us for two weeks in advance. And called the whole thing off. So that was that. Well when you worked with Jimmy Noon, if you could tell a little bit about that. Yeah well I worked with Jimmy Noon. I did some work with him. But when I first come back from Europe I worked with Jimmy in I guess it would be early 33. He got a band together, a new spot open, a very beautiful place on 55th Street, Club Morocco. So I went in there with him. I worked a while with him in there. In fact we worked until the place folded. Yeah. It was a new venture. You ever recorded with Jimmy Noon? I never did. Never made a record with Jimmy Noon. He made some records at the time that I was with him but the company wanted

Preston. So Preston made the record. Are there any other records that you might be on that maybe people don't know about? Of course you don't know what people know but I mean the ones you made under your own name and say the Ma Rainey? And can you think of anything else now that people might not have heard about?

Well I made some with Charlie Creff. I mean I mean. Oh you were on them? Yeah I'm on the Charlie Creff records. And of course with the band in Europe with Sam Wooden's band we made a complete catalog of them. Oh yes all of them. We made many records. But those are all known about but. The other the Charlie Creff do you remember the who else was in the band? Was Zutty with them then? No Zutty wasn't with them then. Zutty was in Chicago then. And Dewey Washington was in Chicago. And Dewey Washington was in the band. And Horace Hewbanks was in the band. And there was a tenor player from Kansas City. I remember the name of the Waddy Walters, he was one of the twins, there was two twin brothers that played. And Lovingood, he played the Boats in New Orleans, he was a terrific pianist, he was with us all the time on the boats.
You were on the boat then one summer, one year about?
Yeah, one season, yeah. And they wanted me to go down to New Orleans to work on the capital with fate, but I was very anxious to get back to Chicago, so I didn't take that.
Now just a couple of minutes if you can tell about your European trip, unless there's something else you can think of too you'd like to tell about.

Well, the European trip was, it was very interesting. I enjoyed it very much. The act that, I went over to join an act that had, it was a dancing act, a Spanish act, and they had a band with them, an American band. I only knew one fellow in the band, Spallin, he was a pianist, had been with the original Jimmy Wade band. So they sent for me, in fact they sent for two of us from Chicago, they sent for Clifford King and myself. And doing the transaction, which it takes quite a bit of transaction, it did at that time from Europe. So in the meantime Clifford had, went to work with Charlie Elgar somewhere and he was doing alright, so he had been looking for us. So he backed down at the last minute. So anyway I went on over alone and joined the band. And of course I didn't know anybody in the band, but this fellow Spallin, the pianist. And after I got there there was a boy that had been here with Sammy Stewart, Roy Butler, he was on the sax and clarinet, he was with the outfit. So it was a very enjoyable trip. I worked with them for a while and the first, our first engagement, well I went directly from here to Bremen and then I had to take a train from Bremen to Hamburg, Germany. I joined them in Hamburg and they were working at a very big elaborate place. And as it would happen at the same time that I got there, Sam Wooden's band was in Hamburg, was in town and of course his band, he was this king of Europe. I mean he's the biggest thing that ever happened because he's the first one that introduced jazz all over there, he went all up in Russia and everywhere. And his name there was, he was like Paul Whiteman was over here at that time. So after the second night that I was there I went out to hear the band and of course there was two of the original members of my band, when I had my band, when I had my band here, Dreamlin in his band, it was Doc Cheatham, Adolph Cheatham, and Jerry Blake, see. And of course Tommy Ladner was in the band. Oh they had a terrific band. And when I heard that band, I mean my heart just went out for it, you know, one of those kind of things. stuff they sent me and made me offer to join the band. Well, that was right where I would want to be with my good friends, you know what I mean? And it was a terrific outfit. So I eventually went on with them and I stayed with them for the, for a period of probably three years, you know.
Is this date about right here? It's a little off.
It's about a year off all the way down. Yeah, it's about a year off all the way down.
You mean it should be a little later or earlier? A little earlier. That's the Esquire Jazz book, so we'll have it on the tape. And you were in Europe, it says here about 1929 to 31 or so.
Yeah, well that's off. I went over in 27, in October of 27. I mean, I gave this to them just from memory, but I went over in October of 27.
So those dates got to be pushed up, they're a little off. Yeah.
It's so hard. I remember those dates back.
Did you work with Tommy Ladner a while over there then?
Yeah, I did. We eventually worked together in a show over there. And we always were friends. Well, I remember Tommy from his Joe Oliver days.

Chicago here, and so when I finally come back to New York, well Tommy got back before I did, and he and Bashir had formed this band, the New Orleans Feet Warmers, you know. So they greeted me with welcome arms in New York. They were working at the Savoy, and they had six pieces of terrific bands, so they wanted me, and he fit right in.
